intro: Learning outcomes describe what someone should be able to do after engaging with courses or materials mapped to this area. They are draft statements for review — not tied to individual assessment questions.

clusters.summary: Builds the everyday data literacy needed to work confidently with information — reading evidence, handling data responsibly and knowing when to seek help.

outcomes.text: Explain what data are, where they come from in your work, and why quality and context matter for sound decisions.
Read common charts, tables and dashboards accurately — identifying trends, limitations and misleading presentation.
Apply basic good practice across the data lifecycle (collect, store, share, retain, dispose) in line with organisational policy.
Describe how your role contributes to responsible data use and recognise when specialist advice is needed.

clusters.summary: Focuses on trustworthy data — improving accuracy and fitness for purpose while meeting ethical, legal and standards obligations.

outcomes.text: Assess whether data are fit for purpose (accuracy, completeness, timeliness, representativeness) and document known limitations.
Apply ethical and legal principles when collecting, using and sharing data — including privacy, security and fair treatment.
Use agreed data standards, definitions and metadata so information stays consistent and interoperable.
Challenge poor-quality or inappropriate data use constructively and escalate issues through the right channels.

clusters.summary: Turns data into insight — framing questions, analysing evidence and communicating findings that support better decisions.

outcomes.text: Frame clear questions that data can help answer and identify what evidence would strengthen a decision.
Apply appropriate analytical approaches to explore patterns, test assumptions and surface actionable insight.
Communicate findings accessibly — separating fact from interpretation and stating uncertainty honestly.
Recommend evidence-based actions and explain trade-offs when data are incomplete or inconclusive.

clusters.summary: Enables safe collaboration — sharing and reusing data across teams and organisations for public value without compromising rights or trust.

outcomes.text: Identify opportunities to share or reuse data that deliver public benefit while respecting legal and ethical duties.
Apply proportionate governance — agreements, access controls and audit — when collaborating across boundaries.
Assess re-identification and misuse risks before sharing and choose safer alternatives where risks are high.
Work effectively with data owners, legal and security colleagues to enable lawful, ethical reuse.

clusters.summary: Builds practical AI literacy and safe everyday use — understanding what AI can and cannot do, spotting opportunities, using approved tools responsibly, and knowing when to stop or escalate.

outcomes.text: Explain in plain language what AI and automation are, including common types (e.g. prediction, classification, generative AI), how they differ from conventional software, and common limitations.
Recognise where AI could improve efficiency or outcomes — and where human judgement must remain central.
Know which AI tools are approved for your work, what data can safely be shared with them, and follow organisational guidance when using them.
Spot when a prompt or task carries a safety risk, adjust or stop before proceeding, and escalate concerns to the right person when something feels wrong.
Identify unreliable AI output and know when to verify, reject or escalate before acting on results.

clusters.summary: Ensures AI is used lawfully, ethically and accountably — interpreting outputs critically and applying governance that protects citizens and the organisation.

outcomes.text: Critically evaluate AI outputs for accuracy, bias and fitness for purpose before acting on or sharing them.
Apply relevant legal and regulatory requirements to AI use in your context (equality, transparency, procurement and records).
Document decisions about AI use — including human oversight, disclosure to citizens and proportionate risk acceptance.
Challenge unethical or non-compliant AI proposals and support governance controls that match the level of risk.

clusters.summary: Covers everyday digital confidence — choosing digital tools, working securely and creating accessible digital content that colleagues and citizens can use.

outcomes.text: Use core digital tools (documents, collaboration, calendars, messaging) efficiently and securely for routine tasks.
Select appropriate digital channels and formats for a task, considering audience, security and record-keeping needs.
Create digital content that meets accessibility standards and plain-language expectations.
Manage your digital footprint responsibly — device hygiene, credentials and recognising common scams or phishing.

clusters.summary: Designs and improves services around user needs — researching, iterating and delivering change that works for diverse audiences.
strands: Making digital services work for everyone

outcomes.text: Map user journeys and pain points for a service or process and identify where digital could improve outcomes.
Apply user research and feedback methods proportionate to the scale and risk of change.
Design or improve services iteratively, testing with diverse users and refining based on evidence.
Balance pace of delivery with inclusion — ensuring changes work for assisted-digital and non-digital users.

clusters.summary: Leads teams in a digital age — building capability, managing transition and aligning digital ambition with organisational priorities.

outcomes.text: Articulate how digital, data and AI can improve team outcomes in line with organisational priorities.
Build team capability and confidence through coaching, role modelling and removing barriers to good practice.
Manage change associated with technology adoption — expectations, training and transition from legacy ways of working.
Make informed trade-offs between innovation, risk, cost and inclusion when championing technology-enabled change.

clusters.summary: Keeps information accurate, current and well governed — knowing provenance, applying controls and correcting mistakes promptly.

outcomes.text: Verify information sources, version control and ownership before using or publishing content.
Apply records management and retention requirements appropriate to your role and information type.
Handle personal and sensitive information in line with classification, need-to-know and secure-sharing rules.
Correct errors promptly and transparently when inaccurate information has been shared.

clusters.summary: Creates the environment where innovation can happen — psychological safety, adaptability and openness to learning from failure.

outcomes.text: Contribute to a team climate where people can raise ideas, experiment and learn from setbacks without blame.
Respond constructively to change and uncertainty — adapting plans when evidence or context shifts.
Recognise personal and team habits that help or hinder innovation and take practical steps to improve them.
Balance delivery pressure with space for exploration proportionate to the problem you are solving.

clusters.summary: Gets to the root of challenges before jumping to solutions — spotting opportunities and building empathy with users.

outcomes.text: Identify problems and opportunities worth solving by combining user insight, data and organisational context.
Frame problems clearly — distinguishing symptoms from causes and defining success in outcome terms.

clusters.summary: Navigates the innovation lifecycle, tests ideas in the real world and communicates results to build support for change.

outcomes.text: Navigate the stages of the innovation lifecycle and use evidence to decide when to refine, stop or scale a solution.
Design small, low-risk experiments that test the riskiest assumptions behind an idea.
Create prototypes (paper, digital or process) that help stakeholders experience and critique a proposed solution.
Gather structured feedback from users and colleagues and use it to refine or pivot proposals.
Document what was learned from testing — including reasons to stop, change direction or proceed.
Tell compelling stories that connect user need, evidence and proposed change for decision-makers and stakeholders.
Build coalitions for change by listening, addressing concerns and aligning proposals with wider priorities.

clusters.summary: Sustains improvement over time — embedding new ways of working, spreading good practice and measuring what matters.

outcomes.text: Establish routines for reviewing performance and acting on feedback after a change goes live.
Spread successful approaches beyond the initial pilot through documentation, coaching and communities of practice.
Identify barriers to adoption (skills, incentives, process, technology) and address them proportionately.
Define simple measures that show whether a change is delivering intended outcomes and adjust accordingly.
